area: Area IV. Takeoffs, Landings, and Go-Arounds
objective: By the end of this lesson you can fly a stabilized approach to a soft or rough field, hold the airplane 1 to 2 feet up in ground effect with a little power, touch down at the slowest possible speed, keep the nose wheel off, and keep rolling until you are off the soft surface.
why: On grass, sand, mud or snow the wheels can sink or the nose wheel can dig in. Letting the wings carry the weight as long as possible protects the gear and keeps you from getting stuck [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

prereading.what: Soft-field approach and landing, and its common errors. This is the core of the lesson.
prereading.label: AFH 9-23 to 9-24

prereading.what: Stabilized approach concept, aiming point, and the go-around gates.
prereading.label: AFH 9-4 to 9-6

prereading.what: Short-field approach speed (also used for soft fields), gust factor, and using power in the flare.
prereading.label: AFH 9-21 to 9-22

prereading.label: PHAK 5-11 to 5-12

prereading.what: Crosswind approach and landing, and crosswind limits.
prereading.label: AFH 9-15 to 9-19

warmup: You are landing on a grass strip that is soft after two days of rain. What would happen if you landed the normal way and let the nose wheel drop, then braked hard?

key_terms.def: A landing surface such as snow, sand, mud, or tall grass that can grab or sink the wheels [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].
An uneven surface that can put big stresses on the landing gear [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].
Less induced drag when the wing is very close to the ground, so the airplane wants to float [[1:108|PHAK 5-11]].
Moving the airplane's weight from the wings to the wheels slowly, using back pressure and power [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].
Stall speed or minimum steady flight speed in the landing configuration [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].
The difference between the steady wind and the gusts. Add no more than half of it to approach speed [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].
A constant-angle glide path to a chosen point at a constant airspeed and configuration [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].
A normal maneuver to stop an approach: power, attitude, configuration [[24:181|AFH 9-10]] [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

chunks.title: What makes a soft-field landing different

body.p: Snow, sand, mud, and tall grass need their own technique. The goal: touch down as smoothly as possible at the slowest possible speed, and let the wings hold the weight as long as practical. That keeps a rough surface from beating up the gear and keeps the wheels from sinking into a soft one [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

The approach looks like a normal approach. The big difference: you keep some power on through the level-off and touchdown. The airplane flies 1 to 2 feet above the surface in ground effect while the speed bleeds off. When the wheels touch, the wings still carry much of the weight, so there is less nose-over force [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

head: Normal landing
Soft-field landing
rows: Normally idle in the round out [[24:179|AFH 9-8]]
Some power through level-off and touchdown [[24:194|AFH 9-23]]
At or just above stall speed [[24:180|AFH 9-9]]
Lowered gently as the airplane slows [[24:180|AFH 9-9]]
Held off; lowered gently only once committed [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]
Used carefully after the nose wheel is down [[24:181|AFH 9-10]]
May need MORE power to keep moving [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]

body.p: Flaps help you touch down slower and are recommended whenever practical. On low-wing airplanes, mud, stones, or slush thrown up by the wheels can damage them. If you used flaps, leave them down on the rollout; full control of the airplane matters more [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

callout.text: Your POH flap setting and speeds come first. If the AFH and the POH differ, the manufacturer wins [[24:172|AFH 9-1]].

check.q: Why do you carry some power through the touchdown on a soft field?
check.a: So the airplane can float 1 to 2 feet up in ground effect while it slows, and the wings still carry much of the weight when the wheels touch [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

body.p: A stabilized approach is a constant-angle glide path to a chosen aiming point, at a constant airspeed and configuration [[24:175|AFH 9-4]]. The aiming point does not move in the windshield. If it moves up toward the horizon you will land short; if it moves down, you will land long [[24:176|AFH 9-5]].

Speed: use the same final approach speed as a short-field landing [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]. That is the POH speed, or not more than 1.3 VSO if there is none. In gusty air add no more than half the gust factor [[24:192|AFH 9-21]]. Extra speed makes you float in ground effect, and floating makes a smooth touchdown harder [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].
Angle: there is no reason for a steep descent unless there are obstacles [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

Energy management means pitch and power together. Too high: less power and lower the nose to hold airspeed, or add flaps. Too low: add power and raise the nose [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. Raising the nose alone to stretch the glide leads to a high sink rate or a low-altitude stall [[24:175|AFH 9-4]]. Do not raise the flaps to fix an undershoot [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

head: AFH stabilized criteria (typical piston airplane)
Target
rows: About a constant 3 degrees to the touchdown zone
Tracks centerline; bank normally 15 degrees or less once on final
+10/-5 KIAS of the AFM speed or 1.3 VSO
Landing flaps as needed, gear down, in trim
Generally 500-1,000 fpm; if over 500 fpm, reduce it before 300 ft AGL
Done before the approach (except the landing checklist)

body.p: Table source: [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

callout.text: Go-around gates: not stabilized by 500 ft above airport elevation in VMC means go around. In a typical piston pattern, go around right away if the approach goes unstable below 300 ft AGL [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

check.q: No POH approach speed is published and VSO is 50 kt. What is the highest final approach speed you should plan in calm air?
check.a: 1.3 x 50 = 65 kt [[24:192|AFH 9-21]]. The ACS allows +10/-5 kt around it (ACS PA.IV.D.S7).

chunks.title: Ground effect, float, and power in the flare

body.p: Near the ground, the surface squeezes the airflow around the wing. Induced drag drops and the airplane wants to keep flying [[1:108|PHAK 5-11]]. The effect is strongest below a height of one wingspan [[1:109|PHAK 5-12]].
Numbers from [[1:108|PHAK 5-11]]. Because drag is lower, any extra speed at the flare means a long float [[1:109|PHAK 5-12]].
The soft-field landing uses this on purpose: a little power plus ground effect lets you hold the airplane just off the surface while it slows [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

bullets: A small amount of power blows more air over the elevator, so you keep pitch authority at low speed. A windmilling propeller at idle can block that airflow and make it hard to flare [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].
Do not chop the throttle too fast. Closing it can cause a sudden increase in sink rate and a hard landing [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].
Ground effect lowers elevator effectiveness and makes it harder to raise the nose [[24:205|AFH 9-34]].
Keep one hand on the throttle for the whole approach and landing [[24:180|AFH 9-9]].

callout.text: Soft field = 'fly it on, don't drop it on.' Wings carry the weight; power and back pressure decide when the wheels take it.

check.q: Why can a power-off flare be harder at very slow speed?
check.a: With no power, less air flows over the elevator, and a windmilling prop can block airflow, so the elevator loses authority [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step (and the ACS tolerances)

body.p: Generic AFH flow. Your POH gives the speeds, flap settings, and power settings.

bullets: 1. Downwind: before-landing checklist done before you reach base [[24:173|AFH 9-2]]. Radio call [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.2]].
2. Base: reduce power, target about 1.4 VSO, flaps as recommended, crab to keep a square ground track [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].
3. Turn final: coordinated, no skid; be reluctant to bank more than 30 degrees this low [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
4. Confirm runway number and alignment, and scan the runway and its surroundings for traffic and obstacles. In doubt, go around [[24:175|AFH 9-4]] [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].
5. Final: landing flaps, POH speed (or not more than 1.3 VSO, plus up to half the gust factor), trim. Pick the aiming point [[24:192|AFH 9-21]] [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].
6. Fly a stabilized, normal-angle approach; correct with pitch and power together [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].
7. Crosswind: wing-low, rudder keeps the nose on centerline [[24:187|AFH 9-16]].
8. Level off and hold the airplane 1 to 2 ft above the surface in ground effect, KEEPING some power on [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].
9. Touch down at the lowest possible airspeed, nose-high, no drift, aligned [[24:195|AFH 9-24]] [[24:180|AFH 9-9]].
10. Hold back pressure to keep the nose wheel off. Use back pressure and power to control how fast weight moves to the wheels [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].
11. Once committed, lower the nose wheel gently; a slight power increase helps ease it down [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].
12. No brakes. Add power if needed to keep moving; do not stop until you reach a firm surface [[24:195|AFH 9-24]] [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].
Any time it is not stable or not safe: go around (power, attitude, configuration) [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

head: What the examiner checks
ACS standard
rows: Manufacturer's published approach speed, or if none, not more than 1.3 VSO, +10/-5 knots, with gust factor applied (ACS PA.IV.D.S7)
Select and aim for a suitable point for the wind, surface, and obstructions (ACS PA.IV.D.S5). No distance tolerance is listed for this Task.
Smooth, timely inputs; nose wheel off until elevator loses effectiveness; proper pitch, minimum sink rate, no side drift, aligned with the center of the runway (ACS PA.IV.D.S9, S10)
Elevator as the manufacturer recommends; exit the soft area at a speed that keeps you from sinking in (ACS PA.IV.D.S11)
Proper control positions and enough speed to keep taxiing on the soft surface (ACS PA.IV.D.S13)
Timely, if you cannot meet these standards or anything makes the landing unsafe (ACS PA.IV.D.S12)

check.q: What is the biggest difference between step 8 here and a normal landing?
check.a: Power stays on through the level-off and touchdown, so the airplane floats 1 to 2 ft up in ground effect while it slows [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

chunks.title: After touchdown: nose wheel, weight transfer, and keep moving

body.p: Tricycle gear: after the mains touch, hold enough back pressure to keep the nose wheel off. Back pressure and power together control how fast the weight moves from the wings to the wheels [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

bullets: If the field is very soft, you can keep the mains just touching while the wings still carry the weight, until you reach a good taxi surface [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].
Until the weight is on the wheels and the nose wheel is down, you can still add full power and take off again, if field length and obstacles allow [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].
Once committed, lower the nose wheel gently. Do not let it 'fall' [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].
No brakes. They load the nose gear and can make the nose wheel dig in. The soft surface slows you enough by itself [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].
On a very soft field you may need MORE power to keep moving and not get stuck [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].
Keep moving with enough power; stopping on mud or snow can bog the airplane down [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

body.p: Tailwheel airplanes: the tailwheel touches with or just before the mains, then firm back pressure holds it down for the whole roll. This fights any nose-over tendency. Brakes are not needed here either [[24:294|AFH 14-8]].

Leave flaps alone on the rollout; staying in full control matters more than cleaning up [[24:194|AFH 9-23]]. When you do clean up later, positively identify the flap control first; pilots have raised the gear by mistake [[24:181|AFH 9-10]].

callout.text: Exiting: at a towered airport, leave the runway at the first available taxiway and do not stop or reverse course on the runway without ATC approval [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21]]. At a non-towered field the FAA discourages back-taxiing because of landing traffic [[17:13|AC 90-66C 10.4.2]].

check.q: Up to what point can you still turn a soft-field landing into a takeoff?
check.a: Until the weight is on the wheels and the nose wheel is on the surface, if obstacles and field length allow [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

chunks.title: Wind and crosswind on a soft field

body.p: You land at the same indicated airspeed in any wind, so wind changes your groundspeed at touchdown and the runway you use [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]. A 10 kt tailwind makes the landing distance about 21 percent longer [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]] [[27:35|AC 91-79B 5.2.9]].

Crosswind methods are the same as any landing. The wing-low (sideslip) method is recommended in most cases: rudder keeps the nose on centerline, and the upwind wing goes down just enough to stop drift [[24:186|AFH 9-15]] [[24:187|AFH 9-16]].

bullets: As you slow in the flare, controls get weaker. Add more rudder and aileron to hold the same correction, and keep the upwind wing down [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].
With wing-low, the upwind main wheel touches first [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].
With rudder-linked nose wheel steering, relax the rudder as the nose wheel touches so you do not swerve [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].
On the roll the airplane wants to weathervane into the wind. Keep adding aileron into the wind; at a stop, hold it fully into the wind [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].
Gusty crosswind: partial flaps and a power-on approach slightly faster than normal, such as normal speed plus half the gust factor (70 kt with 15 kt gusts = 77 kt) [[24:191|AFH 9-20]].

body.p: Limits: airplanes are tested to be controllable in a 90-degree crosswind up to 0.2 VSO. Airplanes certificated after May 3, 1962 show the demonstrated crosswind on a placard [[24:190|AFH 9-19]]. If full opposite rudder cannot stop the turn while holding the needed bank, the wind is too strong for that runway [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].

callout.text: Touching down while drifting puts big side loads on the gear and can cause a ground loop [[24:206|AFH 9-35]].

check.q: Wind from the left. Using wing-low, which wing is down and which main wheel touches first?
check.a: Left wing down; the left (upwind) main wheel touches first [[24:187|AFH 9-16]] [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].

chunks.title: Choosing the runway and the touchdown spot

body.p: Pick the runway for your skill, the airplane, the distance, and the wind. Performance charts assume a paved, level, smooth, dry runway. Surfaces include concrete, asphalt, gravel, dirt, or grass, and the Chart Supplement lists each runway's surface and slope [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]] [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]].

head: Factor
Effect on landing
rows: Less tire friction, but they also act as obstructions and can shorten the roll [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]]
A significant effect on landing distance [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]
Every 10 ft above 50 ft at the threshold
About 16% longer than at sea level [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]

body.p: Touchdown spot: choose a point that suits the wind, the surface, and any obstructions (ACS PA.IV.D.S5). Look for the firmest, smoothest part of the field and a clear path to a firm taxi surface, since you should not stop on the soft part [[24:145|AFH 6-13]] [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

LAHSO: you must be able to land and stop within the Available Landing Distance [[33:253|AIM 4-3-11]]. Student pilots or pilots not familiar with LAHSO should not take part, and the PIC can always decline [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]]. Remember you will not be braking on a soft field [[24:195|AFH 9-24]], so be honest about your stopping distance. Once accepted, a LAHSO clearance must be followed, though a rejected landing is still allowed [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]]. LAHSO needs at least a 1,000 ft ceiling and 3 SM visibility [[33:256|AIM 4-3-11]].

callout.text: The worst combination is high weight, high density altitude, and unfavorable wind [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]. Add a soft surface and you may not have the runway you think you have.

check.q: Where do you find a runway's surface type and slope before you go?

chunks.title: Wind shear, wake turbulence, and planning the go-around

body.p: Wind shear is a sudden, drastic change in wind speed or direction. A headwind turning into a tailwind cuts airspeed and performance [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. A microburst on approach can give a headwind, then a downdraft, then a tailwind, and push you into the ground short of the runway. Microbursts can make downdrafts of up to 6,000 fpm and headwind losses of 30-90 knots [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].
Be ready to go around at the first sign of a microburst; some cannot be escaped at low altitude [[28:266|AWH 22-11]]. Clues: virga at cloud base and a ring of blowing dust [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].

Wake turbulence: every airplane making lift leaves two vortices. They can roll a small airplane faster than its ailerons can fight [[34:147|AIM 7-4-1]]. Strongest behind aircraft that are HEAVY, CLEAN, and SLOW [[34:147|AIM 7-4-3]]. Near the ground they drift sideways at 2 or 3 knots; a 1 to 5 knot crosswind can hold one in the touchdown zone, and a light quartering tailwind needs maximum caution [[34:148|AIM 7-4-4]] [[34:150|AIM 7-4-4]].

bullets: Landing behind a larger aircraft, same runway: stay at or above its path and land beyond its touchdown point [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].
After a larger aircraft's low approach, missed approach, or touch-and-go: wait at least 2 minutes [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].
Avoid the area below and behind the larger aircraft, especially at low altitude, where even a short wake encounter could be catastrophic [[34:151|AIM 7-4-5]].

head: Go-around step
What to do
rows: Full (or max allowable) power, smoothly, right away; carb heat off if applicable [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]
Forward pressure to stop the nose rising, right rudder for torque and P-factor, rough trim; do not climb out of ground effect too soon [[24:182|AFH 9-11]] [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]
Flaps up in small steps; gear up only after a positive rate of climb [[24:182|AFH 9-11]] [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]

callout.text: Two things delay go-arounds: landing expectancy ('it'll work out') and pride [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Decide your go-around point before you start final.

check.q: A larger airplane just did a touch-and-go on your runway. How long does the AIM say to wait?

chunks.title: Traffic, right runway, low-altitude traps, and distractions

body.p: Collision hazards: aircraft on final or landing have the right-of-way. The lower aircraft has it when two are landing, but may not cut in front of one on final [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(g)]]. Straight-in traffic has no priority over pattern traffic [[17:8|AC 90-66C 9.11.1]].

Radio calls at a non-towered field: monitor and self-announce about 10 miles out [[17:13|AC 90-66C 10.4.1]], then report downwind, base, and 'on final for runway [XX]' [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.2]]. Don't announce a sequence number [[17:13|AC 90-66C 10.1]].

Right runway: wrong-surface landings come from unfamiliar airports, complacency, or fatigue. Study the airport diagram first and check runway number and alignment on every final. If in doubt, go around [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].

Stall and spin: a soft-field touchdown happens at the lowest possible airspeed, close to the stall. Overshooting base-to-final and fixing it with inside rudder sets up a skidding, cross-controlled stall that can spin. Go around instead [[24:125|AFH 5-20]] [[13:12|AC 61-67C para 109]].

CFIT and illusions: CFIT is one of the top four causes of GA fatal accidents [[30:22|RMH 3-4]]. A narrower-than-usual runway makes you feel high so you fly too low. Terrain made featureless by snow does the same. Rain and haze also cause low approaches [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]].

Distractions: do checklists early so your eyes are outside on final [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. Many distractions start small and lead to accidents when the pilot stops flying the airplane. Task saturated? Stop, think, slow down, and prioritize [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]], or just go around.

callout.text: Aviate, then navigate, then communicate. In the soft-field float, flying the airplane is the only job.

check.q: You are on final to a narrow grass strip and feel high. What illusion might be fooling you?
check.a: The runway width illusion: a narrow runway makes you feel higher than you are, so you fly too low [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]].

body.p: AFH list of soft-field approach and landing errors [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]:

bullets: Too much descent rate on final.
Too much airspeed on final.
Unstable approach.
Round out too high above the surface.
Poor power management in the round out and touchdown.
Hard touchdown.
Poor control of the weight transfer from wings to wheels.
Letting the nose wheel 'fall' instead of lowering it.

head: Problem
Fix
rows: Flaps, less power, lower the nose; or forward slip. Sink rate over 800-1,000 fpm is excessive [[24:201|AFH 9-30]]
Add power and raise the nose together; never retract flaps; in doubt, go around [[24:201|AFH 9-30]]
Ease into landing attitude as it settles; drifting or long? Go around [[24:203|AFH 9-32]]
Hold the attitude until it settles, maybe a little power; needs a big nose-down? Go around [[24:202|AFH 9-31]]
Some power to cushion it; excessive? Go around [[24:204|AFH 9-33]]
Slight: power to cushion and set landing attitude. Severe: go around now [[24:205|AFH 9-34]]
Sink rate jumps and you land hard; close the throttle slowly [[24:193|AFH 9-22]]
Nose wheel can dig in; hold back pressure and stay off the brakes [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]

callout.text: A 6-inch free fall is roughly a 340 fpm descent, and the landing load can be three or four times the airplane's weight [[24:206|AFH 9-35]]. That is why the soft-field goal is the minimum sink rate.

check.q: Name two soft-field errors that involve the nose wheel or power.
check.a: Poor power management in the round out and touchdown, and letting the nose wheel fall instead of controlling its descent [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

scenario.title: The wet grass strip with a tailwind
scenario.setup: You fly to a non-towered airport with a paved runway and a parallel grass runway. It rained all morning. The grass runway's preferred direction has a light quartering tailwind, but the other direction faces trees at the far end. A local pilot on the radio says the grass is 'a little soft by the windsock.' You are at max gross weight and the field elevation is 3,000 ft. Your CFI wants you to practice a real soft-field landing on the grass.

questions.q: What should you check before you even enter the pattern?
questions.a: POH landing distance corrected for weight, density altitude, and wind, plus the runway surface and slope in the Chart Supplement [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]] [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]]. Snow, ice, or soft ground has a big effect on landing distance [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].

questions.q: Is the tailwind direction a good choice?
questions.a: Usually not. About a 10 kt tailwind adds about 21 percent to landing distance [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]], and your touchdown groundspeed goes up on a soft surface. Land into the wind if the far-end trees and the distance allow, or use the paved runway.

questions.q: Where on the grass should you plan to touch down, and why does it matter?
questions.a: On the firmest part, away from the soft area, with a clear path to a firm taxi surface. Stopping on mud can bog the airplane down [[24:145|AFH 6-13]], and a very soft field may need more power just to keep moving [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

questions.q: On short final you are 10 kt fast and still a little high. What do you do?
questions.a: Extra speed means a long float in ground effect and a harder touchdown [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]. If you cannot get stabilized by the gate, go around [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. Power, attitude, configuration [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

questions.q: Just after touchdown the nose starts to drop and the wheels feel like they are dragging in mud. What now?
questions.a: Hold back pressure to keep the nose wheel off, add power to keep moving, and stay off the brakes [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]. If the nose wheel is still off and the weight is still on the wings, you could add full power and take off, if field length and obstacles permit [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

questions.q: Your passenger starts chatting about the view on final. How do you manage it?
questions.a: Checklists done early so your eyes are outside, and prioritize flying the airplane. When task saturated: stop, think, slow down, prioritize [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].

skills.do: Complete the before-landing checklist before you reach base leg.
skills.practice: Say the checklist out loud on every downwind. Have it done before turning base [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].

skills.do: Make the right pattern calls (or follow tower instructions).
skills.practice: Practice the standard calls: downwind, base, final with the runway number [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.2]].

skills.do: Line up with the correct or assigned runway.
skills.practice: Check runway number and alignment on every final; study the airport diagram first [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].

skills.do: Scan the runway and nearby area for traffic and obstructions.
skills.practice: Scan the runway, the area short of it, and both sides, plus the pattern for traffic, on every final [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

skills.do: Pick and aim for a touchdown point that fits the wind, surface, and obstructions.
skills.practice: Name your aiming point out loud on base; watch whether it moves up or down in the windshield [[24:176|AFH 9-5]].

skills.do: Set landing configuration, airspeed, and trim; adjust pitch and power for a stabilized approach.
skills.practice: Fly approaches to the same visual picture with constant speed and trim; correct with pitch and power together [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

skills.do: Hold the POH approach speed, or not more than 1.3 VSO, within +10/-5 kt, with gust factor applied.
skills.practice: Brief the target speed and gust add before each approach and glance at the airspeed indicator during your scan [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].

skills.do: Keep directional control and crosswind correction all the way through landing and rollout.
skills.practice: Practice the wing-low method down the runway at a safe height, then on full-stop landings [[24:187|AFH 9-16]] [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].

skills.do: Make smooth, timely inputs in the round out and touchdown; keep the nose wheel off until the elevator loses effectiveness.
skills.practice: Practice holding the airplane 1 to 2 ft up with a little power, then holding back pressure after touchdown [[24:194|AFH 9-23]] [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

skills.do: Touch down nose-high at minimum sink rate, no drift, aligned with the center of the runway.
skills.practice: Low passes in ground effect to learn the picture and the power needed; then full landings [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

skills.do: Use elevator as the POH recommends on rollout and leave the soft area at a speed that keeps you from sinking.
skills.practice: On a real grass strip with your CFI, keep the nose light and add power as needed to keep rolling [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

skills.do: Go around on time if the approach goes outside these standards or becomes unsafe.
skills.practice: Have your CFI call random go-arounds at different heights, including in the float [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

skills.do: Keep proper control positions and enough speed to keep taxiing on the soft surface.
skills.practice: Practice continuous-motion taxi on grass with your CFI; avoid stopping on soft ground [[24:145|AFH 6-13]].

quiz.q: What is the main difference between a normal and a soft-field approach?
options: Some power is used through the level-off and touchdown
quiz.why: The approach is like a normal one, but a degree of power is carried through level-off and touchdown [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

quiz.q: How high does the AFH say to hold the airplane in ground effect while the speed bleeds off?
quiz.why: The airplane is flown 1 to 2 feet off the surface in ground effect [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

quiz.q: Which final approach speed does the AFH suggest for a soft-field landing?
options: The same speed used for short-field landings
quiz.why: The short-field final approach speed is equally appropriate to soft fields [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

quiz.q: With no POH speed, VSO 55 kt and gusts 10 kt over the steady wind, the highest target final approach speed you should plan is about:
quiz.why: Not more than 1.3 VSO (71.5 kt) plus no more than half the gust factor (5 kt) = about 77 kt [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].

quiz.q: Why should you avoid braking on a soft field?
options: It can load the nose gear and make the nose wheel dig in
Brakes do not work below 20 kt
quiz.why: Brakes can put a heavy load on the nose gear and cause it to dig in; the soft surface slows you enough [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

quiz.q: After landing on a very soft field, the airplane starts to slow and sink. What may you need to do?
quiz.why: On a very soft field, more power may be needed to keep moving and avoid getting stuck [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

quiz.q: Why should flaps generally stay down during the soft-field after-landing roll?
options: Full control of the airplane matters more than retracting them
quiz.why: Flap retraction is less important than total concentration on maintaining control [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

quiz.q: Which is listed by the AFH as a common soft-field landing error?
options: Holding the nose wheel off too long
Letting the nose wheel fall to the runway
quiz.why: Allowing the nose wheel to 'fall' instead of controlling its descent is a listed common error [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

takeaways: Goal: slowest, smoothest touchdown, with the wings carrying the weight as long as practical.
Fly a normal, stabilized approach at the short-field speed; no steep angle unless obstacles.
Keep a little power on and float 1 to 2 ft up in ground effect; touch down nose-high.
Hold the nose wheel off, lower it gently, no brakes, add power to keep moving.
Until the nose wheel is down and weight is on the wheels, a takeoff is still an option.
Not stable by the gate, wake or wind shear, or any doubt: go around.
cfi_notes: Most common student error: pulling power to idle in the flare out of habit, which drops the airplane in. Have them say 'power stays in' on short final.
Students often let the nose wheel fall once the mains touch. Teach the weight transfer as a continuous back-pressure and power task [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].
Start with low passes in ground effect down a long paved runway to learn the power setting and sight picture before real touchdowns.

Show the difference from the short-field landing: same approach speed, but no steep angle unless obstacles and no braking, where the short-field landing brakes hard [[24:195|AFH 9-24]] [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].
Examiners often probe: when can you still abort and take off from a soft-field landing? Answer: before the weight is on the wheels and the nose wheel is down [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].
Most checkrides are flown on pavement. Have students brief the real-world soft-field plan (surface, firm taxi route, flap damage risk on low wings) orally.
Tailwheel students: tailwheel touches with or before the mains and is held down with firm back pressure [[24:294|AFH 14-8]].
gaps: Airplane-specific numbers (approach speed, flap setting, power setting in the flare, soft-field landing distance corrections) come from the POH/AFM, not these sources.

No source here gives explicit flight-control positions for taxiing on a soft surface (S13) or the manufacturer's elevator recommendation for rollout (S11); AFH 9-24 and 6-13 only say to use back pressure and power and to keep moving. Use the POH and CFI technique.
No source gives grass- or mud-specific landing distance factors; PHAK 11-17 only says soft ground has a significant effect. Some POHs give a grass correction.
Windshear escape technique is in AC 00-54, which is not in these resources.
